title: Multi-tenant cache interference pilot — notes & first-pass results
content:
Summary:

Purpose: quick investigation into how noisy co-tenants affect our KV cache reuse, eviction churn, and downstream paging/memory-bandwidth on Dedicated nodes. We want concrete numbers to decide whether to implement tenant-aware quotas or a soft-hysteresis eviction policy.

High-level finding (TL;DR): under a realistic mixed workload, a moderate noisy tenant (50% of requests but highly divergent context prefixes) reduced effective reuse from ~68% -> ~34% for other tenants, increased eviction rate by ~3x, and caused a 2.5x rise in DRAM read bandwidth as measured inside the host, plus a 4x increase in paging faults on nodes with tight cache envelopes. These effects propagate to 99th-percentile latencies for low-volume tenants.

Experiment setup:
- Hardware: 2x A100-80GB (DGX-style testing rig), NVMe swap enabled for some runs to simulate constrained physical memory, PCIe gen4 interconnect.
- Runtime: serving-runtime branch multi-tenant-probe (commit sha abc1234), lightweight tracing enabled.
- Cache config: global KV cache size=24GB, per-tenant soft limit=none (baseline). TTL disabled. Eviction policy: LRU with batched eviction.
- Workloads (generated):
  - Tenant A (baseline tenants): 10 concurrent streams, chat-like prompts, average sequence length 256, strong prefix reuse (many repeated contexts), target qps per tenant ~80
  - Tenant B (noisy tenant): 25 concurrent streams, synthetic random prefixes (low reuse), average seq length 128, target qps ~160
  - Background synthetic traffic: small inference bursts to simulate occasional admin jobs
- Measurement tools: perf counters (cpu), nvprof/nsys for device metrics, iostat for NVMe, /proc/vmstat for pageins, custom runtime telemetry (reuse counters, eviction counters, per-tenant residency map).
- Runs: 6x stable 30-minute runs per configuration (baseline single-tenant, multi-tenant mixed, multi-tenant with per-tenant cutoffs).

Key metrics definitions (as instrumented):
- reuse_rate = fraction of token generation steps where a KV lookup hit returned a resident block (weighted by token count)
- eviction_rate = number of KV pages evicted / minute
- paging_events = major page faults + swap-ins observed by host
- tail_latency_p99 = 99th percentile token generation latency measured at the SDK level
- host_read_bw = MB/s read bandwidth on DRAM channels correlated to KV activity (estimated via perf counters + runtime correlation)

Results (representative numbers):
1) Baseline (Tenant A only)
   - reuse_rate: 68%
   - eviction_rate: 42 evictions/min
   - paging_events: 0.4/min
   - host_read_bw: 420 MB/s
   - tail_latency_p99: 98 ms

2) Mixed (Tenant A + noisy Tenant B, no tenant limits)
   - reuse_rate (Tenant A): 34% (-50% relative)
   - reuse_rate (Tenant B): 12% (expected)
   - eviction_rate: 132 evictions/min (+3.1x)
   - paging_events: 1.6/min (+4x)
   - host_read_bw: 1050 MB/s (+2.5x)
   - tail_latency_p99 (Tenant A): 240 ms (+2.45x)

3) Mixed + soft per-tenant hard-cap (prototype): cap Tenant B to 8GB cache residency, eviction policy unchanged
   - reuse_rate (Tenant A): 58% (much recovered)
   - eviction_rate: 64 evictions/min
   - paging_events: 0.6/min
   - host_read_bw: 540 MB/s
   - tail_latency_p99 (Tenant A): 112 ms

Observations / interpretation:
- Cross-tenant interference is primarily a residency/contention problem, not just bandwidth: eviction churn correlates strongly with the fraction of unique prefixes generated by Tenant B.
- Bandwidth increase tracks eviction rate: more evictions -> more cold fetches from model/state -> more DRAM/GPU transfers.
- Paging events spike when combined working set exceeds physical host memory minus other processes; eviction churn amplifies swap activity if NVMe is enabled (this is worst-case and depends on host configuration).
- LRU alone is unfair to stable tenants because high-throughput noisy tenants can continuously push out hot blocks before they get reused (classic thrashing).
- Our current instrumentation (per-tenant residency map) is sufficient to attribute most evictions to the noisy tenant, but short-lived collisions still make attribution noisy at sub-second granularity.

Micro-profiles (nvprof/nsys highlights):
- PCIe stalls: measurable during eviction-heavy bursts; host->device transfers queued and backpressure observed (latency spikes aligned with NVMe swap-ins in the worst runs).
- Kernel execution was stable; the bottleneck is memory traffic and prefetcher effectiveness on resident/evicted pages.

Small reproducible test (toy):
- Script: tests/kv_interference/toy_noisy_runner.py (see linked PR)
- Behavior: two co-located simulators (one with high unique prefixes) cause eviction spike and measurable tail-latency increase in <90s on a local dev machine. Useful for CI-style regression tests.

Mitigations tried (short experiments):
1) Tenant-aware soft quotas (simple cap per tenant): worked well in our pilot; recovered reuse for stable tenants at cost of throughput for noisy tenant. Implementation complexity: low.
2) Hysteresis-based eviction (rare eviction window): reduce eviction rate by delaying eviction of blocks aged <X seconds even if LRU says evict. Tradeoff: larger memory footprint, but helps stable tenants. Complexity: medium (requires per-block timestamps + background sweeper).
3) Admission control (reject or throttle new requests from noisy tenant when cache pressure high): effective but customer-visible. Needs policy and SLO guardrails.
4) Background warmup / prefetch for active tenants during idle cycles: helps reduce cold misses after eviction-induced churn. Complexity: medium-high; must be bandwidth-aware.

Quick cost/benefit:
- Per-tenant soft quota: engineering ~2-4 engineer-weeks, rollout toggled per-customer. Likely highest ROI and lowest user-facing risk.
- Hysteresis eviction: 4-6 engineer-weeks + more runtime complexity; good as complementary measure to reduce oscillation.
- Admission control: policy + infra changes, potential revenue/CS impact; consider as last resort.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How well do per-tenant quotas interact with Dedicated nodes where tenants may have reserved capacity? Should quotas be tenant-priority weighted?
- Fine-grained cost attribution: can we connect eviction churn to token-unit cost increases for customers? (useful for billing tie-ins).
- Could we do proactive tenant fingerprinting to classify noisy vs. stable workloads and apply automatic policies? Risk: misclassification and false throttling.
- Can we compress cold blocks (lightweight quantized storage) instead of evicting to reduce bandwidth? Evaluate compression/decompression CPU overheads.
- Need to test on AMD/Intel host platforms and upcoming CPU memory topologies; current results are A100-centric.

Immediate next steps (short horizon):
- Ship a lightweight per-tenant soft quota prototype behind a feature flag (PROJ-1123). Target: 2 sprints for a minimal implementation (enforce residency cap + telemetry). Owner: Aisha.
- Add CI toy test in the linked PR so regressions trigger. Owner: Noah.
- Run a second round of experiments with NVMe off and with larger physical memory to isolate swap contribution. Owner: Marcus.
- Draft design doc for hysteresis eviction with perf cost modeling. Owner: Elena.

Attachments / artifacts captured:
- nsys traces: multi_tenant_run_2025-02-15.qtrace (on GDrive>traces)
- runtime telemetry dump: resident-map-2025-02-15.json (sanitized)
- heatmaps: eviction-heatmap-02-15.png, reuse-trajectory-02-15.png
- toy test: tests/kv_interference/toy_noisy_runner.py (see PR #487)

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Consider exposing a per-tenant "cache hint" from SDK (customers can tag traffic as high-reuse) — may help better default behavior for PLG customers.
- We should instrument per-tenant bytes transferred over PCIe to directly measure cross-device bandwidth pressure (current host_read_bw is an estimate).
- Coordinate with SRE to get metrics from Dedicated nodes in staging fleet for a week to validate at scale.

References / links:
- Linked PR with prototype enforcement: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/487
- Design notes (confluence): confluence://SERVE-Cache-Playbook
- Jira Epic: PROJ-1123

If we want to present this to product/CS as a first-pass decision, recommendation is to prioritize per-tenant soft quotas + telemetry, then iterate on hysteresis.

-- Marcus
